explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says Satan "…incited David to take a census of Israel." (1 Chronicles 21:1). David is Israel's king, and the push to start counting comes from Satan. A headcount sounds harmless, but this one is where the trouble starts.
No battle plans in this one. Verse 1 says Satan incited David, Israel's king, to take a census of Israel. The only thing on the move is a counting job. It sounds quiet, but it turns into a big deal.

No ark in this passage, friend. What Satan stirs David up to do is take a census of Israel (1 Chronicles 21:1). David is Israel's king, and he gets a counting project instead of a parade. That headcount is where everything in this story begins.

explanations.answer: He asks why David would bring guilt on Israel
explanations.explanation: That's it. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), asks, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). He's the guy in the meeting who says "Are we SURE about this?" while everybody else is already picking up their pens. He even asks, "…are they not all servants of my lord?"

explanations.answer: He says the troops are too worn out to travel
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions tired troops. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), goes right at the order itself. He says, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). His worry is the guilt, not the road.

explanations.answer: He asks David to wait until after the harvest
explanations.explanation: Joab never talks about timing. He doesn't ask David for a later date, he questions the whole idea. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), says, "Why should he bring guilt on Israel?" (1 Chronicles 21:3). He wants the count stopped, not scheduled.

Not this time, friend. The text says, "Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab." (1 Chronicles 21:4). Joab speaks up, and David keeps the order anyway. So Joab goes out and does the counting.

Right. Joab pushes back, but "…the king’s word prevailed against Joab." (1 Chronicles 21:4). David doesn't call anything off. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), travels through Israel and then returns to Jerusalem.

Yes, Levi. The text says Joab "…did not include Levi and Benjamin in the count…" (1 Chronicles 21:6). Two tribes get skipped. The same verse gives the reason: the king's command was detestable to Joab.

Ephraim isn't the one named. The tribes Joab leaves out are Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:6). Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves them out of the count. The text never says Ephraim was left out.

Asher isn't the one. Verse 6 names the tribes Joab leaves out: Levi and Benjamin (1 Chronicles 21:6). Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves them out, and the text says the king's command was detestable to him.

That's what the text says. Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves out Levi and Benjamin "…because the king’s command was detestable to him." (1 Chronicles 21:6). He carries out the order, but he's clearly not at peace with it. Joab argued against it from the start (1 Chronicles 21:3).

It's true, friend. The text gives the reason right away: "…the king’s command was detestable to him." (1 Chronicles 21:6). Joab, David's army commander (1 Chronicles 27:34), leaves out Levi and Benjamin for that reason. He had already asked David why he wanted to do this (1 Chronicles 21:3).

David doesn't do that, friend. After God strikes Israel, David says to God, "I have sinned greatly because I have done this thing." (1 Chronicles 21:8). He puts it on himself, not on Joab. He also asks God to take away his iniquity.

Right, no blame goes to Joab. David says to God, "I have sinned greatly because I have done this thing." (1 Chronicles 21:8). He takes it on himself and says he "…acted very foolishly." There's no pointing a finger anywhere else.

Yes, baker. The LORD instructs Gad, David's seer, to go and tell David, and the message is, "I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you." (1 Chronicles 21:10). David has to pick one. The three are three years of famine, three months of being swept away before his enemies, or three days of the sword of the LORD (1 Chronicles 21:12).

explanations.answer: A way to undo the census
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't offer to undo it. Through Gad, David's seer, He says, "I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you." (1 Chronicles 21:10). The choice is among three outcomes.

explanations.answer: Forty days to make it right
explanations.explanation: No forty days here. The offer through Gad, David's seer, is "three options" (1 Chronicles 21:10). They come with numbers, but they're three years, three months and three days (1 Chronicles 21:12).

explanations.answer: To fall into the hand of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's his pick. David says, "Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men." (1 Chronicles 21:13). He also says he's deeply distressed, and I think that's an honest thing to say.

explanations.answer: To fall into the hands of his enemies
explanations.explanation: David says the opposite. He asks, "…do not let me fall into the hands of men." (1 Chronicles 21:13). Three months of being swept away before enemies was one of the three options, but he doesn't choose it. He asks to fall into the hand of the LORD.

explanations.answer: To face three years of famine
explanations.explanation: Famine was one of the three (1 Chronicles 21:12), but David's answer doesn't mention it. He says, "Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great…" (1 Chronicles 21:13). That's the answer he gives Gad.

Yes, mercies. David says, "…for His mercies are very great…" (1 Chronicles 21:13). He's in a tight spot with three hard options, and what he leans on is the LORD's mercy. I think that says a lot about what he knows of God.
David isn't talking about armies. He's trying to stay out of the hands of men, and he says, "…for His mercies are very great…" (1 Chronicles 21:13). The word is mercies. That's what he trusts.
David isn't shopping for supplies here. What he says about the LORD is, "…for His mercies are very great…" (1 Chronicles 21:13). The word is mercies, and that's the reason he gives for his choice.

The LORD doesn't let it keep going. Verse 15 says He saw it and "…relented from the calamity…" and told the angel, "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" (1 Chronicles 21:15). The angel is stopped right there.
Right. The LORD saw it, "…relented from the calamity…" and said to the angel, "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" (1 Chronicles 21:15). The angel doesn't get to keep going. The LORD stops him.
Yes. David and the elders, "…clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown." (1 Chronicles 21:16). The elders are Israel's leaders, and they go down on their faces together. This is a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: Run to hide inside the city walls
explanations.explanation: They don't run. The text says that David and the elders, "…clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown." (1 Chronicles 21:16). They're on their faces, not looking for cover.

explanations.answer: Send for the priests to bring the ark
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention the ark or the priests here. David lifts his eyes and sees the angel, and then David and the elders, "…clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown." (1 Chronicles 21:16). They go down on their faces.

That's what he asks. David says, "O LORD my God, please let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house, but do not let this plague remain upon Your people." (1 Chronicles 21:17). He asks for it to land on himself and his family instead. I think that's a shepherd's heart, since he calls them "these sheep."

It's true, friend. David prays, "…please let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house, but do not let this plague remain upon Your people." (1 Chronicles 21:17). He asks for it to fall on himself and his family, not the people. He's the one who gave the order, and he says so.

Yes, Ornan. The angel of the LORD orders Gad, David's seer, to tell David to build an altar "…on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite." (1 Chronicles 21:18). A threshing floor is where grain gets separated from the husks. David goes up at the word Gad spoke in the name of the LORD (1 Chronicles 21:19).
Boaz isn't in this story, friend. The text names the owner of the threshing floor: Ornan the Jebusite (1 Chronicles 21:18). That's where David is told to build the altar.
Nabal doesn't show up here. The altar goes on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (1 Chronicles 21:18). The message comes through Gad, David's seer, from the angel of the LORD.

That's it. Ornan sees the angel, and "…his four sons who were with him hid themselves." (1 Chronicles 21:20). Ornan is the one working the threshing floor. I think they were scared stiff, but that part is just my guess.

explanations.answer: They run to tell the king
explanations.explanation: The text gives the sons a different action. It says that "…his four sons who were with him hid themselves." (1 Chronicles 21:20). Telling the king isn't part of that verse. Then David comes to Ornan, and Ornan bows facedown before David (1 Chronicles 21:21).

explanations.answer: They bow down to the angel
explanations.explanation: The bowing in this scene comes later. The sons "hid themselves" (1 Chronicles 21:20). The one who bows facedown is Ornan, and it's before David (1 Chronicles 21:21).

explanations.answer: He offers to give David all of it
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ornan says, "Take it! May my lord the king do whatever seems good to him." (1 Chronicles 21:23). Then he offers the oxen, the sledges and the wheat, saying, "…I will give it all." David won't take it for free, though, and says he insists on paying the full price (1 Chronicles 21:24).

explanations.answer: He asks for twice the full price
explanations.explanation: Ornan does the opposite of haggling. He says, "Take it! May my lord the king do whatever seems good to him." (1 Chronicles 21:23). He doesn't ask for a coin. He offers it all.

explanations.answer: He says the land isn't his to sell
explanations.explanation: Ornan doesn't say that. His answer is, "Take it! May my lord the king do whatever seems good to him." (1 Chronicles 21:23). He treats the land as his to give, and he offers David all of it.

explanations.answer: He won't give offerings that cost him nothing
explanations.explanation: That's his reason, in his own words. David says, "…I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing." (1 Chronicles 21:24). Ornan's gift is generous, but David wants the offering to be his own. So he pays.

explanations.answer: He thinks Ornan's oxen are too old to offer
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about the oxen's age. David gives his reason out loud: "…I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing." (1 Chronicles 21:24). It's about the cost, not the oxen.

explanations.answer: He wants the priests to bring the wood
explanations.explanation: Priests and wood deliveries don't come up. The wood Ornan offers is the threshing sledges, and David turns down the whole gift. He says, "…I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing." (1 Chronicles 21:24).

Fire it is. David "…called upon the LORD, who answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering." (1 Chronicles 21:26). He paid full price, built the altar, and the LORD answered right there.
No rain in this scene. The text says David called on the LORD, "…who answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering." (1 Chronicles 21:26). The answer came down as fire.
No bread falls from the sky here. The LORD "…answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering." (1 Chronicles 21:26). It's fire, and it lands on the altar David just built.

That's exactly how it goes. "Then the LORD spoke to the angel, who put his sword back into its sheath." (1 Chronicles 21:27). It comes after the fire from heaven on David's altar. The angel who had a drawn sword over Jerusalem puts it away.
It's true, friend. The text says, "Then the LORD spoke to the angel, who put his sword back into its sheath." (1 Chronicles 21:27). The sword that was drawn over Jerusalem goes back in.

explanations.answer: Here will be the house of the LORD God
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel." (1 Chronicles 22:1). He picks out this threshing floor, where he built the altar. It's the same site he paid Ornan for (1 Chronicles 21:25).

explanations.answer: Here will be the palace of the king
explanations.explanation: David isn't building himself a palace on this spot. He says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel." (1 Chronicles 22:1). It's for the LORD.

explanations.answer: Here will be a city for the Levites
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. David says, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel." (1 Chronicles 22:1). The spot is for the LORD's house and the altar.
